Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-extra1-prompt-long-0469", "row_sha256": "4b1048192db4b4f749490de93a346ef28850315ad55e055229669f4b7d616200", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you help me write a practical setup plan for the Bell family photo archive? Nora and Sam Bell live in Tacoma with Leah, who is twelve, and Owen, who is eight. They are trying to put family pictures in one place without making the everyday import routine complicated. Nora says, “I want the pictures easy to find, but I don’t want another account that quietly sends everything somewhere.” Sam says he would rather have a slightly slower local copy than discover later that a folder was skipped. Make the plan about their actual setup, not a generic overview of photo libraries.

Their main storage box is a small four-terabyte NAS called Cedar in the hallway cupboard. The family uses a laptop in the dining room to import pictures. The intended archive folder is /volume1/FamilyPhotos/Incoming. Nora’s Android phone and Sam’s Android phone each have several years of pictures, and an older iPhone has some pictures from before Leah was born. They also have a digital camera that writes to SD cards, plus scans of prints from Nora’s late grandmother June. Those scans are currently in a folder called June scans on the laptop. Don’t assume that all devices use the same import method or that the older iPhone is still used every week.

They want the new arrangement to be understandable to all four family members. Leah sometimes photographs school projects and wants to find those pictures later, while Owen mostly takes short videos of the dog. Nora sorts pictures by year and family event when she has time, but she does not want the setup to require her to rename every file. Sam would like imported items to retain their original dates when the camera or phone has recorded them. Mention how duplicates and uncertain dates should be handled without pretending the archive can identify every duplicate or repair every missing date automatically. The family has not chosen a tagging system, so don’t invent a required set of tags.

There is a 2 TB external drive named Porchlight. Sam connects it to the laptop most Sundays and sometimes forgets if they have been away for a weekend. The family wants it treated as a backup destination, not as a second place to sort pictures by hand. Explain where that backup fits in the workflow and avoid suggesting that Porchlight is continuously connected. They have not said that it contains an existing archive, so do not describe overwriting or migrating existing files. They do want to understand what would happen if a backup run is skipped because the drive is not plugged in.

For imports, use a clear conditional action and an explicit alternative. If Cedar is reachable on the home network when the laptop importer starts, copy the new items into the Incoming folder and verify the copied files with checksums before reporting that the import is complete. If Cedar is not reachable at that time, leave the new items on their original phone, SD card, or laptop import staging location, queue a retry, and do not mark the items as archived. Keep that alternative distinct from the reachable-NAS action; do not imply that a failed connection means files should be deleted or that the importer should silently proceed as if the copy succeeded. Explain in plain language what the family should see in either case.

They prefer local storage because the archive includes family pictures and scans. Use this configuration block as part of the proposed setup, exactly as written:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 18
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"
The retention value applies to the local archive’s temporary import staging area, not to the organized family collection. The family has not asked for old photographs to be deleted after eighteen days. Since remote access is disabled in the block, do not recommend enabling cloud upload or remote sharing in the plan. If the family later asks about remote access, explain that this setting would need to be deliberately reviewed first; don’t treat that possible future discussion as permission to switch it on now.

Please cover basic organization without turning the project into a large cataloguing job. The family would like a year-based structure, with optional event folders where someone already knows the event name. Keep the Incoming folder as the destination for newly copied items, and describe how it can later be reviewed and organized without changing the source files’ recorded dates. The family does not want the plan to require facial recognition. Make the distinction between a copy in the archive and a copy on Porchlight understandable, and say that a successful import alone is not the same as a verified backup. Don’t promise protection against every kind of loss.

Could you arrange the answer so it is useful when Nora and Sam sit down at the laptop? Start with a short description of the intended flow, then include a numbered section for the first setup and a separate explanation of the import decision and its two branches. Include the exact configuration block, explain which folder the retention setting concerns, and finish with a practical note about the weekly external-drive backup and the case where Porchlight is absent. Keep the tone calm and plain, include the two family quotes above as ordinary context, and distinguish known details from anything the family would still need to choose. Don’t present configuration steps as already completed; they are asking for a plan they can review, not reporting that the archive has been set up.", "output": "Write a practical, plain-language setup plan for the Bell family photo archive, based on the details below. Do not present any configuration as already completed. The family is asking for a plan to review.

## Family and equipment
Nora and Sam Bell live in Tacoma with Leah, age twelve, and Owen, age eight. Their small four-terabyte NAS, named Cedar, is in the hallway cupboard. They use a laptop in the dining room to import pictures, and the intended archive destination is `/volume1/FamilyPhotos/Incoming`.

The family’s sources include Nora’s Android phone and Sam’s Android phone, each with several years of pictures; an older iPhone containing pictures from before Leah was born; a digital camera that uses SD cards; and scans of prints from Nora’s late grandmother June. The scans are currently in a laptop folder called `June scans`. Do not assume all devices use the same import method or that the older iPhone is still used every week.

Nora says, “I want the pictures easy to find, but I don’t want another account that quietly sends everything somewhere.” Sam says he would rather have a slightly slower local copy than discover later that a folder was skipped. Keep these preferences in view and make the plan specific to the family rather than a generic overview.

## Organization and handling
The setup should be understandable to all four family members. Leah sometimes photographs school projects and wants to find those pictures later; Owen mostly takes short videos of the dog. Nora sorts by year and family event when she has time, but does not want to rename every file. Sam would like imported items to retain their original recorded dates where available.

Suggest a year-based structure with optional event folders when someone already knows the event name. Newly copied items should go to `Incoming` and can be reviewed and organized later without changing their recorded dates or source files. Explain how to handle possible duplicates and uncertain dates without claiming every duplicate can be identified or every missing date repaired automatically. The family has not selected a tagging system, so do not require particular tags. Do not require facial recognition.

## First setup and local archive
Include a numbered section for the first setup. Explain the role of the laptop, Cedar, and the `Incoming` folder, and distinguish a copy in the archive from a copy on the external backup drive. Make clear that a successful import by itself does not mean the backup has been verified, and do not promise protection against every kind of loss.

Include this configuration block exactly:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 18
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

Explain that `retain_days = 18` applies to the local archive’s temporary import staging area, not to the organized family collection. The family has not asked for old photographs to be deleted after eighteen days. Because remote access is disabled in this configuration, do not recommend cloud upload or remote sharing. If the family later asks about remote access, explain that the setting would need deliberate review first; that possible future discussion is not permission to enable it now.

## Import decision
Explain the following decision in plain language, keeping its two branches distinct:

- If Cedar is reachable on the home network when the laptop importer starts, copy the new items into `/volume1/FamilyPhotos/Incoming` and verify the copied files with checksums before reporting the import complete.
- If Cedar is not reachable then, leave the new items on their original phone, SD card, or laptop import staging location, queue a retry, and do not mark them as archived.

Explain what the family should see in either case. A connection failure must not result in deleting source files or silently treating an unsuccessful copy as complete.

## Porchlight backup and closing note
The family has a 2 TB external drive named Porchlight. Sam connects it to the laptop most Sundays, though he sometimes forgets when they have been away for a weekend. Treat Porchlight as a backup destination, not a second place to sort pictures by hand, and do not describe it as continuously connected. The family has not said it contains an existing archive, so do not propose overwriting or migrating files already on it. Explain where the backup fits in the workflow and what happens if a run is skipped because Porchlight is not plugged in.

Finish with a practical note about the weekly external-drive backup and the absent-drive case. Keep the tone calm and clear, preserve the difference between known details and choices the family still needs to make, and include the two family quotes above as ordinary context."}]
